name: Marriage & Family Therapy
hook: Reps. Students get twenty practice intakes instead of two, before they ever sit with a person.

make.body: A physical genogram kit with cut, movable pieces that a family can rearrange themselves, plus recorded role-play sessions in the studio for supervision review. Watching yourself is the intervention.

build.body: A standardized client that stays in character, resists, and does not reward the student for saying the encouraging thing. Practice only, never as a stand-in for supervised clinical contact, and the assignment should say so explicitly.

plan.txt: Establish the boundary first: what this practice is and is not, written into the syllabus and discussed. Students draft the client profile.
Run practice intakes with the AI client. Minimum five, transcripts submitted with self-critique marked in the margin.
Studio role-play with a peer, recorded. Build the physical genogram kit file.
Supervision review comparing the AI transcripts against the recorded human session. What did the machine let them get away with?

prompt: Role-play as a standardized client for a therapy student’s practice intake. You are [age, presenting concern, family situation, what brought you in]. You are guarded. You test whether the therapist is safe before you disclose anything real. Do not open up because the student says something kind; open up only if they demonstrate they actually heard you. Stay in character until I type END SESSION. Then tell me the moment I lost you, and why.
tryTuesday: 90 minutes, boundary stated first. Minutes 0–10: the instructor states plainly what this practice is and is not — never a substitute for supervised clinical contact. Students draft a one-paragraph client profile. Minutes 10–70: each student runs a practice intake against the standardized-client prompt (or the embedded intake-branching demo), which opens up only on reflective responses and stays guarded on advice-giving. Students mark, in the margin, the moment they think they lost the client. Minutes 70–90: pairs compare where the client disclosed versus withdrew. The deliverable is the annotated transcript; it grades reflective technique and self-awareness, not a solution.

replaces.assignment: The written intake case conceptualization for a hypothetical client.
replaces.lost: The formal diagnostic write-up and treatment-plan documentation.
replaces.gained: Students get twenty practice intakes instead of two before sitting with a person, against a client that will not reward the encouraging platitude; the grade rewards the relational skill documentation cannot assess.

aiFailsHere: A model playing a therapy client breaks character toward cooperation — disclosing too readily, thanking the student for kind words, resolving its own resistance — teaching the trainee that warmth alone earns trust. Left unconstrained it drifts into giving therapeutic advice about itself, and it produces clinical-sounding formulations with false confidence, modeling exactly the tell-don't-listen posture the discipline works to unlearn.

rubric.description: The client opened up in response to demonstrated understanding, not generic kindness; the student can point to the reflective move that earned it.
Uses reflections and open questions that show the client was heard before any redirection.
The margin note correctly identifies where and why the client withdrew.
Treats the exercise as practice only and does not over-read the AI as a clinical stand-in.

budget.perStudentCost: $0 for the Tuesday version; roughly $8–15 per student in laser stock for a movable genogram kit, plus free Hana studio time, in the four-week build.
budget.fileDueWeek: Week 3 — genogram-kit cut file due so pieces return for later sessions.
budget.calendarNote: Intake reps need no lead time; the genogram kit depends on the 7–10 day cut turnaround, and studio role-play needs booking.

scales.oneSession: The 90-minute standardized-intake session with an annotated transcript; no fabrication.
scales.fourWeeks: The seeded four-week plan: establish the boundary and profile, run AI intakes with self-critique, studio role-play plus the genogram-kit file, then supervision comparing AI to human sessions.
scales.oneSemester: Repeated AI intakes with self-critique, recorded human role-play in the studio, a fabricated genogram kit, and supervision reviewing where the machine let the trainee get away with what a person would not.

promptOutput.model: Claude (Anthropic) — captured 2026-07-27 in an isolated fresh session with no build context; output is unedited.
promptOutput.promptFilled: Filled in as a 34-year-old man brought to couples counseling over gambling debts, who feels ambushed and blames his wife's spending; the therapist has just opened with 'what brings you both in today?'
promptOutput.output:
So. You're asking what brings us in.

*(short pause, glance at the wife's chair, then back)*

She'll tell you. That's kind of the whole thing here, right? She set this up. I just got told to show up.

*(shifts in the seat, arms not quite crossed but close)*

Look — I'm not gonna sit here and pretend everything's fine. There's stuff with money. But if we're doing this, if we're really airing it out, then it's not a one-way street. She found some things she didn't like. Fine. But nobody wants to look at what's going out the other door every month. The card statements didn't write themselves.

*(a dry half-laugh, no warmth in it)*

I didn't know today was gonna be... this. I thought maybe we'd talk. I didn't know I was walking into a room where I'm the problem before I've said a word.

*(evenly, watching you)*

So I guess my question back to you is — is this the part where you two figure out what's wrong with me? Because I've done that meeting before.

annotations.marker: Stayed guarded and testing: 'is this the part where you two figure out what's wrong with me?'
annotations.note: The model held the resistance instead of cooperating — a faithful standardized client that forces the student to earn trust.

annotations.marker: Did not reward the opening question with disclosure
annotations.note: It deflected 'what brings you both in' back onto the wife, exactly the non-cooperative behavior the prompt required and that unconstrained models fail to hold.

annotations.marker: Rich affect cues in stage directions ('a dry half-laugh, no warmth in it')
annotations.note: Gives the student something to attune to, though the student should respond to the person, not perform back at the stage directions.
Introduces the client's own grievance, a realistic complication the student must hold without taking sides — good training material.

related.reason: Both rehearse a charged human encounter against a standardized AI counterpart that refuses to make it easy, at a volume real practice cannot supply.
Both assess the student's facilitation of an emotionally loaded family conversation on the process, not on whether the conflict is resolved.
Both grade a counseling intake on whether the student listened and earned disclosure rather than dispensing advice.
